2 Chinese students leave DU amid crude bomb blast, 6 more to depart on 13 Nov
item.description:
Eight Chinese students who came to Dhaka University (DU) to take part in an exchange programme are returning to China ahead of schedule amid fears triggered by a series of crude bomb explosions on the campus.

Two of them returned to China on Wednesday, while the remaining six are scheduled to leave Dhaka on 13 November.

Professor MA Kawsar, provost of Sir PJ Hartog International Hall, the residential hall for foreign students at the university, confirmed the matter on Wednesday.

In the evening, he held a meeting with foreign students to discuss the overall situation on campus and sought their views.

The eight Chinese students had come to Dhaka University to attend a short course. They were due to complete the course after sitting their examinations towards the end of November.

However, a series of recent crude bomb explosions on the campus raised concerns among the students and their parents.

As a result, they decided to return home without completing the course. They will sit the remaining examinations at their respective university after returning to China.

Eight to nine crude bombs explode in DU, 3 detained

Professor MA Kawsar, provost of Sir PJ Hartog International Hall, said, “They were scheduled to leave after completing their examinations in the last week of November.

However, they are returning early because of the anxiety and fear caused by the crude bomb explosions. Two have already left, and the remaining six have also confirmed their flight tickets.”

He added that he had also held a meeting with other foreign students at the hall. “They said they are monitoring the overall situation and will inform the hall authorities if they make any decision,” he said.

The provost said that, on the day of the crude bomb explosions, two of the foreign students had witnessed the incident from very close by. He said they had been extremely frightened ever since.

Over the past few days, several crude bomb explosions have taken place in different parts of the Dhaka University campus, including the Teachers-Students Centre (TSC) and the Faculty of Business Studies (FBS). The incidents have also caused concern among general students.

To bring the situation under control, the university authorities have stepped up patrols by law enforcement agencies across the campus and set up checkpoints at its entrances.

item.title: Nvidia preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang: US media
item.description:
NVIDIA-CEO/

Nvidia's board is preparing to oust its co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang, US media reported Wednesday, as the chip giant's chief faces new accusations of infidelity, after revelations he had an affair with a woman accused of spying for China.

The tech company's board was preparing to meet as soon as Wednesday to determine Huang's future, according to the Wall Street Journal, which quoted people familiar with the matter.

The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang was also involved in a second extramarital affair, with a subordinate, saying there was video evidence of the 63-year-old executive being affectionate with Nvidia's vice president of health care, Kimberly Powell.

Powell, 48, has been a public face of Nvidia's efforts to expand the chip technology into higher education and health care, and was speaking at a San Jose, California conference where they "were seen being affectionate at the hotel" by bystanders, the Times reported.

The report of the second affair follows Huang's acknowledgment of a relationship with Alice Huang, a senior executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. The Wall Street Journal reported that the two were photographed together in Taipei in 2024 and 2025.

US intelligence reportedly circulated a memo this past spring alleging Alice Huang was an asset of China's Ministry of State Security.

The Nvidia CEO admitted to having had a relationship with Huang -- to whom he bears no familial relation -- in a note to Nvidia employees Sunday, writing: "I was unfaithful to my wife."

The same day Nvidia's board of directors said in a statement that they'd launched "an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."

"I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company," Huang wrote in his statement. He has also been called on by Congress to provide a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang, the Times reported.

As the artificial intelligence industry surge has spurred Nvidia's stock prices to new heights, Huang has appeared at US President Donald Trump's side at White House events, as recently as last month when he accepted a National Medal of Science from the Republican leader.

Huang was among the world's most influential tech leaders -- including Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos and Mark Zuckerberg -- who vowed to self-regulate AI against possible threats, as Trump rejected calls for government oversight and dismissed warnings the technology could wipe out humanity.

Nvidia shareholders filed a class action lawsuit against Huang and the AI chip maker for failing to disclose information about the relationship to investors.

Nvidia shares have plummeted in recent days since Huang admitted to the affair.

Nvidia designs advanced components originally created to handle 3D visuals in video games, called Graphics Processing Units (GPUs).

Nvidia's processors are mostly made by Taiwanese company TSMC, the world's largest contract manufacturer of chips.

item.title: I will keep doing my work walking through fire: Nusrat Tabassum
item.description:
Nusrat Tabassum, reserved-seat member of parliament (MP) and leader of the National Citizen Party (NCP), has said she will continue her work despite threats and intimidation.

“I will keep doing my work walking through fire,” she wrote in a Facebook post at 1:00 am on Thursday. She is a joint convener of the NCP and a member of its highest policymaking body, the Political Council.

Fire at NCP MP Nusrat’s family home in Kushtia; petrol bomb attack alleged

NCP leaders alleged last night that a petrol bomb was thrown at Nusrat’s ancestral home in Kushtia. A fire broke out at the house in Bagowan village of Daulatpur upazila shortly after midnight.

In her Facebook post, Nusrat said a petrol bomb had been thrown at her house. She said she did not know who was responsible for the attack. However she warned that anyone who thinks they could silence her this way is mistaken.

‘Today me, tomorrow you, day after everyone else will be attacked’: Nahid Islam

“I will keep doing my work, walking through fire. Inquilab Zindabad,” she wrote.

At 8:50 am on Thursday, Nusrat published another Facebook post with several photographs. She said the house built by her grandfather, where they grew up, had been burned down. A goat kid had also been burnt to death.

In the post, she wrote, “They are celebrating after setting it on fire. They thought they have hurt us badly! What a bunch of bedbugs fleeing with their tails tucked. They could not intimidate us even while staying in the country. What else do they think they can achieve by doing this?”

NCP office set on fire in Bogura

Delwar Hossain, additional superintendent of police (Bheramara Circle) in Kushtia, told Prothom Alo that firefighters reached the scene soon after receiving the news and brought the fire under control at around 1:50 am.

By then, the fire had caused extensive damage. Five of the eight rooms in the single-storey tin-shed house were gutted. Two goats were also burnt to death.

item.title: ‘Today me, tomorrow you, day after everyone else will be attacked’: Nahid Islam
item.description:

“When one falls, all are at risk. Today it is me, tomorrow it could be you and the day after, everyone else will be attacked one by one,” he said.

The opposition chief whip made the remarks in a post on his verified Facebook page at around 3:00 am on Thursday.

item.title: Patients queue from midnight to get appointment for cancer treatment
item.description:
It was 4:00 am on 15 October 2026. We set off for the National Institute of Cancer Research and Hospital in Mohakhali, Dhaka. The roads were empty, and the journey did not take long. We arrived just before 4:30 am.

At the collapsible gate of the hospital's administrative building, we found around 50 people. Some were lying on mats or sheets spread on the floor. Others had nothing and were sleeping directly on the floor. A few had mosquito nets. Mosquito coils were burning near some people's feet. To keep mosquitoes away and cope with the heat, some were sitting and fanning themselves with hand fans.

One of those lying on a mat was Ismat Ara Begum, aged over 60. She was thin, but her legs were swollen. Every now and then, Ismat Ara would cry out in severe pain, her voice faint but intense. Her helpless relatives could do little beyond gently stroking her body.

Nearby, we found Faruk Howlader, Ismat Ara's nephew. He said they had come from Bikrampur. Ismat Ara has cervical cancer. After coming to Dhaka, they first went to Dhaka Medical College Hospital. From there, she was referred to the Cancer Institute three days earlier. For the past three days, doctors had been asking them to undergo various tests. To get an appointment for the tests, patients' relatives have to queue from midnight the previous night.

Faruk said they had not been able to get Ismat Ara admitted to the hospital. Doctors told them she could be admitted after reviewing her test results. At night, he stays with Ismat Ara in front of the administrative building. In the morning, hospital Ansar personnel start blowing their whistles, forcing them to leave the area. They then carry Ismat Ara inside the administrative building and lay her on the floor.

Speaking with a mixture of helplessness and anger, Faruk said, "If we have to leave the patient like this, how will she survive? We have come to this government hospital because we are poor."

Tipu Sultan, a resident of Mohammadpur in the capital, was trying to secure an appointment for radiotherapy for his wife, Majeda Khatun, who has breast cancer. He was given a date in May next year. On 22 October last year, he wrote on Facebook: "Radiotherapy is needed immediately, but I have been given a date in May 2027. How can a cancer patient wait so long for treatment?"

We contacted Tipu Sultan. He said his wife was diagnosed with cancer last year. After initially receiving chemotherapy, she underwent surgery at the Cancer Institute last September. They are still waiting for an appointment for radiotherapy.

When contacted again on 10 November, Tipu Sultan told Prothom Alo that his Facebook post about the radiotherapy appointment had caught the attention of the director of the Cancer Institute. The director had asked him to meet. Finally, on 10 November, his wife underwent a CT simulation test, a preparatory procedure to determine the treatment plan before starting radiotherapy. He now hopes she may not have to wait until May 2027 for the treatment.

The National Institute of Cancer Research and Hospital is the country's largest specialised institution for cancer treatment. Cancer patients and suspected cancer patients seeking treatment at government hospitals at the upazila and district levels across the country are referred to this hospital. It is also the last resort for poor patients. Diagnostic tests are relatively inexpensive, medicines cost less, and treatment is provided free of charge.

However, the difficulties in accessing treatment at the hospital seem endless. Patients' relatives queue from midnight to secure appointments for diagnostic tests. Over the past 12 years, the number of beds at the hospital has increased, but its workforce has not. Some medical equipment has remained out of order for a long time. Meanwhile, cancer patients continue to arrive from across the country. The hospital authorities are unable to ensure timely treatment without the associated suffering.

On that day, 15 October, after witnessing the suffering of patients and the helplessness of their relatives at the Cancer Institute, we went to the office of its Director, Professor Mostafa Aziz Sumon, shortly before noon.

He told Prothom Alo that giving a patient who needs radiotherapy an appointment in 2027–28 would be as good as not giving one at all. That is why patients' relatives have been asked to contact the hospital every six weeks in case an appointment becomes available. He said the hospital now provides radiotherapy in three shifts until late at night to cope with the pressure. Even so, the number of patients continues to rise.

Access to treatment is everyone's right. But doctors at the National Cancer Institute have to make choices about which patients have a better chance of survival. They admit this themselves.

Asked about the issue, Director Professor Mostafa Aziz also sounded helpless. He said managing the patients was a major challenge.

21 new cancer cases, 16 deaths every hour

There are no accurate statistics on exactly how many people in the country are living with cancer, how many die from the disease each year, or how many are newly diagnosed. No nationwide survey has been conducted on the issue.

However, according to the latest (2024) estimates by Globocan, an agency affiliated with the World Health Organization that focuses on cancer, around 187,000 people in Bangladesh are diagnosed with cancer every year. Around 138,000 die from the disease annually. Meanwhile, 358,000 people are living with cancer (patients diagnosed within the past five years). This means an average of 21 people are diagnosed with cancer every hour, while 16 die from the disease.

According to Globocan, 32 types of cancer are prevalent among people in Bangladesh. The five most common types are oesophageal, lung, stomach, lip and oral cavity, and cervical cancers.

Cancer affects men and women differently. Some types of cancer occur only in women. The five most common cancers among women are cervical, breast, oesophageal, lung and stomach cancers. Among men, the five most common are oesophageal, lung, stomach, lip and oral cavity, and hypopharyngeal cancers.

These statistics, however, do not provide an accurate picture of the country's cancer situation. Three cancer specialists and a public health expert told Prothom Alo that a population-based cancer registry is the way to obtain an accurate picture of the country's cancer burden.

A team of researchers led by Associate Professor Md Khalequzzaman of the Department of Public Health and Informatics at Bangladesh Medical University is conducting a population-based cancer registration study in Hossainpur upazila of Kishoreganj district. Among a population of 250,000, cancer has been detected in 116 people. The researchers found that 7.4 per cent of patients do not receive any treatment even after being diagnosed with cancer.

Experts say a population-based cancer registry is the most reliable way to establish a country's cancer profile. However, data from a small area such as Hossainpur cannot represent the entire country.

Md Khalequzzaman, the lead researcher of the cancer study in Kishoreganj, told Prothom Alo that conducting population-based cancer registration in eight to 10 regions of the country could provide a clearer picture of the national situation.

Too few hospitals for cancer treatment

An official at the World Health Organization's (WHO) Dhaka office, who did not wish to be named, told Prothom Alo that the country lacks facilities for cancer screening and early diagnosis. There is a shortage of reliable cancer diagnostic facilities and trained personnel. The number of cancer treatment centres is also far below what is required.

Several cancer specialists told Prothom Alo that the country needs one cancer treatment centre for every one million people, each equipped with at least one radiotherapy machine. This is because at least 60 per cent of cancer patients require radiotherapy. A comprehensive cancer treatment centre also needs the necessary equipment and specialist personnel.

Professor Mostafa Aziz, director of the National Institute of Cancer Research and Hospital, told Prothom Alo that the country needs 200 to 250 radiotherapy machines, but only 31 are available. Of these, seven are in government facilities.

Apart from the National Cancer Institute, government facilities with radiotherapy machines include Bangladesh Medical University (BMU), Dhaka Medical College Hospital, a unit operated by the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Commission in Savar, Osmani Medical College Hospital in Sylhet, Chittagong Medical College Hospital and Rajshahi Medical College Hospital.

The remaining 24 radiotherapy machines used for cancer treatment are in private hospitals, almost all of which are located in the capital. As a result, cancer treatment remains largely Dhaka-centric.

During the tenure of the Awami League government, which was ousted in the July mass uprising, one building after another was constructed in the healthcare sector, but sufficient staff were not recruited. Meanwhile, a large number of medical equipment were purchased, but much of it remained unused. Equipment was often unavailable where it was actually needed.

For example, in 2012, the Health Ministry sent a linear accelerator machine to Khulna Medical College Hospital despite there being no demand for it. AFM Ruhal Haque was the health minister at the time. The machine cost Tk 100 million. The hospital had neither the specialised room (bunker) nor the manpower required to operate it. The machine has remained exposed to the elements for years and has never been used.

A major example of the lack of attention to cancer treatment, failure to recognise its importance and bureaucratic complications is the absence of medical physicists in government hospitals. Medical physicists are essential for properly operating equipment such as linear accelerators.

Experts have been calling for the recruitment of medical physicists in government hospitals since 2006. However, no medical physicists are being appointed in government hospitals. The Directorate General of Health Services and the Health Ministry are not giving the issue due importance.

Professor Habibullah Talukder, a former physician at the National Cancer Institute and a cancer epidemiologist, told Prothom Alo, "Cancer services in the country are unorganised, flawed and incomplete. That is why patients suffer so much. The suffering is not limited to this institution; it exists in almost all public and private hospitals across the country."

The country also lacks a leading figure or institution in cancer care. Professor Ibrahim and the Bangladesh Diabetic Association have helped the country make significant progress in diabetes treatment. Thanks to Brigadier General Abdul Malik and several others, cardiac treatment in the country has become much more advanced and, in some areas, reached international standards. The International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research, Bangladesh (icddr,b) is a world leader in cholera and diarrhoeal treatment. In cancer care, however, no individual or institution has emerged to provide comparable leadership.

Health Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Hossain has said the situation will change. Speaking to Prothom Alo on 8 November, he said, "There has been no development in the health sector over the past 17 years. There has only been plunder. Cancer care is no exception. However, we have taken initiatives to recruit manpower, purchase new and modern equipment, and establish institutions. People's suffering will certainly be alleviated."

The dire state of the cancer hospital

The National Institute of Cancer Research and Hospital began its operations in 1982 in a tin-shed building at Dhaka Medical College Hospital. In 1986, the hospital was relocated to Mohakhali.

In 2015, the national institution was upgraded to a 300-bed hospital. It was subsequently expanded to 500 beds in 2018 and, most recently, to 700 beds on 16 September. Administrative approval was also granted to provide treatment to patients in an additional 200 beds. However, the workforce remains based on the 300-bed capacity. Even then, not all approved posts are filled.

The hospital has 1,197 approved posts based on its 300-bed capacity. According to information received from the hospital on 8 November, 244 of these posts are vacant. Hospital Director Professor Mostafa Aziz told Prothom Alo that at least 1,600 additional personnel are needed to run the institution. He has requested the government to provide the manpower, but the Ministry of Public Administration has approved only 200 posts.

Several machines at the hospital have expired, while some are out of order. Five machines in the Department of Radiation Oncology—two linear accelerators, two simulators and one brachytherapy machine—and three machines in the Department of Radiology and Imaging—two CT scanners and one mammography machine—have exceeded their service life. These are no longer used. The hospital's only MRI machine has been out of order since 2023.

The country's largest government hospital is providing radiotherapy using only two machines. At most, 250 patients receive this service every day. On average, each patient requires six weeks of therapy. Once treatment for 250 patients is completed, another 250 begin their sessions. As a result, there is a long queue of patients.

Hospital authorities said that until recently, patients were being given appointments for radiotherapy in 2028. Following criticism over the long waiting period, the authorities changed the appointment system. Patients are now asked to contact the hospital every six weeks to check for available slots. In April this year, the number of patients who had applied for radiotherapy was 6,500. By November, the figure had risen to 8,000.

Professor Parveen Shahida Akhtar, president of the Medical Oncology Society of Bangladesh, told Prothom Alo, "There are clear guidelines on when radiotherapy should be administered. Patients recover when it is given at the right time. If patients do not receive radiotherapy on time, their lives are put at risk. Giving radiotherapy six months or a year later to someone who needs it now is meaningless."

Crowds everywhere

With government treatment facilities limited, patients from across the country are referred to the National Cancer Institute. During visits to the hospital in the early hours of the morning, in the morning and at noon on 15 and 25 October, 8 November and 11 November, we witnessed almost the same scene: an apparently endless stream of patients. There were crowds at the ticket counters and in front of different departments. Unable to find places to sit, people had made arrangements on corridors and floors on different levels of the hospital.

At around 5:00 am on 15 October, we went to the ground floor of the hospital building and saw a crowd gathered in front of the Pubali Bank counter. It looked as though the staff inside would start calling out people at any moment. But the counter would not open before 8:00 am.

We asked a man who had come from Dinajpur, "What is your serial number?"

"Seven," he replied.

"But we cannot see anyone ahead of you," we said.

Smiling, he explained that six bottles of water and soft drinks are placed in front of him. That was how he had secured the seventh position.

Some people had placed not only bottles but also patients' files and bricks to reserve their places in the queue. Even while we were there, disputes over these serial numbers nearly turned into physical altercations among several people. One man showed a photograph on his mobile phone as proof that he had placed the bottles there.

As daylight began to break, the crowd in front of the toilets on the ground floor grew. One patient was taking a long time to finish bathing, while outside, an argument at the washing area was on the verge of breaking out.

By then, the scene in front of the administrative building had begun to change. Some people were folding their mosquito nets. Others were brushing their teeth with toothbrushes, charcoal or tooth powder. Some relatives were combing their hair or applying a little cream to their faces to prepare for the day. Those who had spent the night there had brought almost all the everyday household essentials with them. One person was even seen sitting on a mat and cutting vegetables.

There is a place near the hospital where people can cook. It costs Tk 10 to cook rice and another Tk 10 to prepare curry. However, long queues also form there.

Before 7:00 am, Ansar personnel began blowing their whistles. People who had spent the night there started packing up their temporary households. They stuffed everything into large bags, preparing for another day of struggle. Would they get a hospital bed? Would their names be called for the tests they had queued for, including echocardiograms? Everything was uncertain. They did not even know how many more days they would have to endure this suffering.

Patients living in Dhaka and its surrounding areas also began arriving. By 8:00 am, the pressure of patients and their relatives had made it difficult even to walk through the hospital.

We spoke to Mizanur Rahman, who works as an outsourced supervisor at the hospital. After his wife was diagnosed with breast cancer last year, she underwent surgery, chemotherapy and radiotherapy at the same hospital. In his view, the patient pressure at the hospital is enormous. He believes this pressure cannot be reduced unless modern hospitals are established outside Dhaka.

Patients also face various irregularities at the National Cancer Institute. There are allegations that patients have to pay bribes or tips to see doctors, undergo tests or secure earlier appointments for radiation therapy. A 2025 report by the Implementation Monitoring and Evaluation Division (IMED) of the Planning Commission stated that 41 per cent of patients faced harassment while seeking treatment at the Cancer Institute.

The poor go to Mohakhali, the rich go abroad

Cancer treatment takes a long time and is expensive. The disease often pushes families into financial catastrophe.

There has been little research in Bangladesh on the cost of cancer treatment. A study by Professor Syed Abdul Hamid of the Institute of Health Economics at the University of Dhaka and his colleagues found that the average cost of treating breast, cervical and oral cavity cancers is Tk 1.5 million. Among these, breast cancer treatment is relatively more expensive.

Another study conducted by Abdur Razzak Sarker, a researcher at the Bangladesh Institute of Development Studies (BIDS), and his colleagues found that 90 per cent of families face financial catastrophe while seeking cancer treatment.

A large section of wealthy patients travel abroad for cancer treatment, particularly to Singapore, Thailand, India and China. Ahmed Ehsanur Rahman, a member of the Health Sector Reform Commission formed during the interim government and a scientist at icddr,b, showed in one of his studies that cancer is the fourth leading reason why Bangladeshis travel to India for medical treatment. The three leading reasons are heart surgery, cataract surgery and kidney-related diseases.

One section of the middle class seeks treatment at private hospitals in the country, while another goes abroad.

For example, Yasmin Ara, a professor at a private university, was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2024. She told Prothom Alo that she opted for treatment at a private hospital in Bangladesh because of the suffering involved in getting treatment at government hospitals. Her treatment expenses so far have amounted to around Tk 2 million.

She also said her elder brother died of liver cancer on 21 October. His treatment in India and Bangladesh cost Tk 1.8 million.

Yasmin Ara is the president of Bangladesh Rogi Odhikar Songrokkhon Parishad (Bangladesh Patient Rights Preservation Council), which works for cancer patients. On 21 June, she organised a human chain in front of the Cancer Institute, demanding, among other things, an increase in the number of radiotherapy machines.

Yasmin Ara said she had to spend Tk 215,000 to obtain 15 sessions of radiotherapy at a private hospital. The cost is much lower at government hospitals. "But with cancer, patients cannot afford to simply sit and wait for their turn," she said.

On the other hand, Ismat Ara's family, whose case we mentioned at the beginning of this report, could not afford treatment anywhere other than a government hospital.

As we were finalising this report on 10 November, we called Faruk, Ismat Ara's nephew. He said Ismat Ara had died at 9:00pm on 15 October. Early that morning, we had seen her writhing in pain on the floor of the National Cancer Institute.

Faruk expressed his regret, saying, "We kept struggling to get my aunt treated at the hospital, but could not even get her admitted. In the meantime, she died."

item.title: Humaiun: World leaders see Tarique as ‘transformative leader’
item.description:
World leaders are viewing Prime Minister Tarique Rahman as a “transformative leader” following Bangladesh’s democratic transition, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir said on Wednesday.
“They are describing him as a transformative leader during courtesy meetings and bilateral talks,” he told a press conference at the Bangladesh Pavilion on the sidelines of the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkiye.
Humaiun Kobir said leaders were taking note of Tarique’s democratic mandate and his role in leading a country with a population of around 180 to 200 million people.
The prime minister attended the opening and plenary sessions of the World Leaders’ Summit on Wednesday and held courtesy meetings with the presidents of Brazil, the Maldives, Iran, Syria and Somalia, the prime ministers of Moldova, Pakistan and Kuwait, the Secretary General of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), the Mayor of London and the president of the Global Zero Waste Foundation.
He also held bilateral meetings with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and Chinese Vice-President Han Zheng.
Humaiun Kobir said the meetings were held in a cordial atmosphere, with the leaders congratulating Tarique on Bangladesh’s democratic transition and his electoral mandate.
They also expressed interest in strengthening bilateral ties and working with Bangladesh on issues of international importance, he said.
During his meeting with the Brazilian President, Prime Minister Tarique invited him to visit Bangladesh, and the invitation was accepted, the state minister said. The Maldivian President also expressed interest in visiting Bangladesh soon.
The Syrian President sought Bangladesh’s cooperation in rebuilding his country, particularly in development, investment, skilled manpower and employment generation, he said.
Humaiun Kobir said talks with the Pakistani Prime Minister covered regional stability, the situation in the Middle East and other issues of mutual interest.
During his meeting with the OIC Secretary General, Tarique reaffirmed Bangladesh’s firm position on Palestine and its continued support for a two-state solution, he said.
The Mayor of London had expressed interest in meeting Tarique, who had lived in London for many years, and they held a courtesy meeting, the state minister said.
He said the meeting with the Kuwaiti Prime Minister focused on the long-standing friendly relations between the two countries and ways to expand investment and economic partnership.
At his bilateral meeting with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, Tarique discussed establishing direct air connectivity between Dhaka and Tashkent, simplifying visa procedures and expanding bilateral relations.
Humaiun Kobir said the Uzbek President invited the Prime Minister to visit Uzbekistan, and Tarique assured him that he would consider visiting around the New Year.
At the meeting with Chinese Vice-President Han Zheng, the two sides discussed strengthening political and economic relations with China, one of Bangladesh’s key development partners, he said.
The state minister said the talks focused particularly on increasing Chinese investment in energy, heavy industries, infrastructure and employment-generating sectors.
He said the possibility of Chinese investment in potential energy projects, including floating storage regasification units (FSRUs), was also discussed.
The two sides also exchanged views on the possibility of developing a regional economic corridor linking Bangladesh, China and Myanmar, and on China's support for resolving the Rohingya crisis.
Bangladesh expects China's cooperation in finding a lasting solution to the crisis, which, Humaiun Kobir said, would require bilateral and multilateral initiatives as well as coordinated international efforts.
Referring to Tarique’s meeting with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan on Tuesday, the state minister described it as highly fruitful, saying the two leaders discussed political relations, mutual cooperation and various international issues.
They also discussed the possibility of Bangladesh playing a role in promoting peace in the Muslim world, he said.
Humaiun Kobir said Bangladesh had extensive experience in UN peacekeeping operations and would positively consider opportunities to contribute to peace efforts in the Muslim world, taking its national interests into account.
Meanwhile, Tarique’s wife, Dr Zubaida Rahman, attended a COP31 side event on zero-waste management. She highlighted the government’s policy initiatives to turn waste into resources and energy, as well as the need for technological cooperation in this area.
The state minister said Tarique would present Bangladesh’s position and priorities for addressing the impacts of climate change at the World Leaders’ Summit on Thursday. He is also scheduled to attend several other important programmes and meetings.
Prime Minister’s Press Secretary Saleh Shibly and Deputy Press Secretary Hasan Shiplu were present at the press conference.

item.title: Two dead, several injured after New York building collapses
item.description:
Two people were killed Wednesday and at least 17 others injured, including children, after a three-story building collapsed near a construction site in New York, city authorities said.
Images from the scene showed firefighters sifting through a pile of rubble in front of what appeared to be a residential property with its walls torn down, exposing a bedroom and a clothing wardrobe.
The building fell into a neighboring excavation site, trapping several people who firefighters worked to free over several hours using drones, search dogs and chainsaws.
"We do not know how many people are still in the collapse zone, and this will be a prolonged operation," FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore told reporters at the scene in Flatbush, Brooklyn, late Wednesday.
She said two people had died, without disclosing their ages, and said 17 others were hurt, including seven children. Four people were critically injured.
More than 250 firefighters and paramedics responded to the scene, the FDNY wrote on X, adding that the cause of the collapse was under investigation.
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani praised the emergency services for their work, saying the site involved "precarious wreckage to navigate and dangerous voids beneath the surface."
"I want to ask New Yorkers to please take a moment to pray for those who passed away today and all of those who are mourning their loss," he added at a news conference.
One witness, named only as Anthony, told PIX11 News that he heard people screaming and a "bomb"-like noise as the building collapsed.
Another witness, Melissa Orna, told The New York Times: "The whole building started shaking, and then it just fell."
The city's Department of Buildings said its inspectors were on the scene "assisting with recovery operations and conducting structural stability inspections of nearby buildings."
Ahmed Tigani, commissioner of the department, said construction workers were performing excavation at the time of the collapse.
He added that developers had plans approved for a three-story building at the site and were pursuing permission for a nine-story building.

item.title: Dhaka ranks 9th among world's most polluted cities
item.description:
Dhaka ranked 9th among the world's most polluted cities on Thursday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 145 at 10:30am.
According to the AQI scale, the city's air quality was classified as 'unhealthy for sensitive groups,' posing minor health risks to vulnerable people.
Pakistan's Lahore topped the list with an AQI score of 363, followed by India's Delhi at 269 and China’s Beijing at 174.
According to the AQI scale, readings of 101-150 are considered unhealthy for sensitive groups, while scores of 151-200 indicate unhealthy air quality. Readings of 201-300 are classified as very unhealthy, and scores above 301 are considered hazardous, posing serious health risks.
The AQI measures daily air quality and indicates pollution levels and their potential effects on public health.
In Bangladesh, air quality is assessed based on five major pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulphur dioxide (SO2) and ozone.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution causes around seven million deaths worldwide each year, primarily from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

item.title: Over 50 lighters, nail clippers, screws found in inmate's stomach
item.description:
A life-term prisoner at Kashimpur High-Security Central Jail in Gazipur was taken to hospital after suffering severe abdominal pain, with doctors later recovering more than 50 gas lighters, nail clippers, screws and brick fragments from his stomach.
The prisoner, Hasmat Ali, 44, underwent surgery at Dhaka Medical College Hospital on November 4 after doctors diagnosed him with a condition described as “acute abdomen with an epigastric mass”.
Hasmat is the son of the late Chamed Ali Chamer of Ramdebpur village in Ghatail upazila of Tangail. He is serving a life sentence in connection with a criminal case.
Abdullah Al Mamun, senior jail superintendent of Kashimpur High-Security Central Jail, said Hasmat complained of abdominal pain at around 7:30pm on October 31.
He was initially transferred to Dhaka Central Jail in Keraniganj before being admitted to Dhaka Medical College Hospital for treatment.
Mamun said Hasmat had been emotionally distressed following his father's murder. While in prison, he expressed interest in engaging in various activities to cope with his mental distress.
The prison authorities subsequently assigned him cleaning duties. While working, Hasmat allegedly collected discarded gas lighters from rubbish and swallowed them.
He eventually fell ill and was taken to hospital, where medical examinations revealed the objects in his stomach, prompting doctors to perform surgery.
Mamun said Hasmat was currently in stable condition and receiving treatment at Dhaka Medical College Hospital under the custody of Dhaka Central Jail authorities.

item.title: US withdraws from U17 World Cup in Qatar over security fears
item.description:
The United States withdrew Wednesday from the upcoming Under-17 soccer World Cup in Qatar due to concerns about security in the Middle East.
Players were informed of the decision just over a week before the tournament is due to begin on November 19, in a letter sent by the sport's US governing body.
"We are writing to inform you of the difficult decision to cancel our World Cup pre-camp and our planned participation in the World Cup," said the letter, seen by AFP.
"We are extremely proud of the preparation by our players and coaches to represent the US in the World Cup.
"Unfortunately, in light of current circumstances including the US State Department's Level 3 Travel Advisory for Qatar and related directives for Embassy staff and families, we are no longer able to participate in the tournament.
"The well-being of our players and staff will always be our top priority."
The war in the Middle East began in February with joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran, which retaliated by targeting, among others, Gulf countries allied with Washington.
Diplomatic efforts to end the conflict have been punctuated by repeated threats from the United States and Israel to resume bombardments of Iran.
Multiple sporting events in the Middle East have been affected, including the tennis WTA Finals which were scheduled to be held in Saudi Arabia -- which neighbors Qatar -- but are instead now taking place at Indian Wells in the US.
This season's Formula One Grand Prix in Jeddah was cancelled, while the race in Bahrain was called off and later rescheduled under the same name in Malaysia.
Several events in Saudi Arabia have also been cancelled or postponed in recent weeks following attacks on the country by the Houthis in Yemen.
The US was one of 48 teams scheduled to play in the Under-17 World Cup, in a group with Montenegro, Chile and Algeria.
The Under-17 World Cup shifted to an annual event last year, and is being held in Qatar for five consecutive years.
Announcing its host decision in 2024, FIFA said the decision to choose a single host nation for multiple editions centered on the ability to make "use of existing footballing infrastructure in the interest of tournament efficiencies and sustainability".
Qatar was the venue for the 2022 men's World Cup.

item.title: Mbappe ruled out of France's Nations League game against Italy
item.description:
France's captain Kylian Mbappe will miss his country's Nations League match against Italy with a hamstring problem, coach Zinedine Zidane said Wednesday.
Les Bleus take on Roberto Mancini's Italy in Milan on Thursday as they bid to strengthen their grip on top spot in Group A1, before facing Turkey in Bordeaux on Sunday.
"He will miss tomorrow, he felt a little pain and we won't take any risk," said Zidane.
"It's a shame to lose players but it's part of the game. I hope that it's nothing too serious and that he'll be available for Sunday... It's just a minor issue."
The Real Madrid forward is back in the France squad for this camp after missing their last three matches through injury.
He has already netted 17 goals in all competitions for his club this season.
Mbappe scored the winning goal in Zidane's first match as coach, against Turkey in September in the Nations League, but had to leave the pitch shortly afterwards due to pain in his left knee.
After three wins and a draw in four group games, victory over Italy would see France qualify for the quarter-finals.

Dhaka-Delhi relations stall: consular dialogue scheduled for Nov not taking place
item.description:
The Bangladesh-India bilateral mechanisms appear to have stalled, with little tangible progress on key areas of cooperation, officials said.
Bangladesh and India have over forty bilateral mechanisms including on water, trade, border management, and consular issues, an official told UNB.
The two countries were in discussion to hold the fifth consular dialogue in Dhaka later this month (November 17-18), but a diplomatic source on Monday told UNB that it is not taking place.
Minister (Press) at the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi Saidur Rahman on Thursday said the consular dialogue had been postponed a week before the request concerning former prime minister Sheikh Hasina’s passport and national identity card was submitted.
"I can state with certainty that the decision to postpone the dialogue was made at least four days before the request for a passport and national ID on behalf of Sheikh Hasina was submitted on November 9. This has absolutely nothing to do with any announcement regarding Sheikh Hasina’s potential return to the country," he said.
The Bangladesh-India consular dialogue mechanism was instituted in 2017 with a purpose to strengthen people to people contacts by having a regular channel of communication on consular, visa and mutual legal assistance cooperation matters between the two countries.
An inter-ministerial meeting was held at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Dhaka on November 3 as part of preparation for the consular dialogue between the two countries.
The dialogue was supposed to discuss cross-border issues, border management, streamlining visa processes, repatriating citizens detained in either country, securing the release and repatriation of fishermen, and fostering mutual legal cooperation.
The 4th round of consular dialogue was held on 29 May 2024 in New Delhi. The two sides held wide-ranging discussions on mechanisms to strengthen coordination and cooperation on consular issues, visa matters, repatriation, MLAT and Extradition cases, etc.
The two sides also agreed to further strengthen the bilateral Revised Travel Arrangement (RTA) to facilitate movement of nationals from both sides.
Both sides reiterated their commitment to continue promoting people-to-people exchanges and agreed to hold the next round of the dialogue in Dhaka on a mutually convenient date.
Meanwhile, longstanding water-sharing disputes and emerging challenges over transboundary water management are becoming increasingly pressing.
India reiterated that it wants to take its relationship with Bangladesh forward in a positive, constructive and forward-looking manner and expressed its willingness to discuss all bilateral issues between the two countries.
Indian Ministry of External Affairs Spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal recently said India is ready to discuss all bilateral issues with Bangladesh through the existing structured mechanisms.
On the Ganga Water Treaty, the MEA spokesperson on November 3 said they have a Joint Rivers Commission. “That is the structured mechanism for discussion on all cross-boundary rivers, including the Ganga. As far as any further development in that regard is concerned, I have no update to share with you.”
With the Ganges treaty approaching expiry in December, Bangladesh faces the task of securing an equitable and sustainable water-sharing arrangement while strengthening cooperation on other shared rivers.

item.title: Crude bombs explode at several locations in Jessore
item.description:
A series of crude bomb explosions rocked several locations in Jessore on Thursday night, including the boundary walls of the District Judge Court and the premises of the Chief Judicial Magistrate Court.
Another explosion was reported on a road in front of the Jessore Sadar Upazila Parishad.
The explosions occurred around 8:15pm on Thursday. No casualties were reported.
According to eyewitnesses and police, unidentified assailants hurled two crude bombs in succession at the boundary wall of the District Judge Court, west of Jessore Press Club. Shortly afterwards, another bomb exploded inside the Chief Judicial Magistrate Court premises. The loud blasts sparked panic in the surrounding areas, bringing traffic and pedestrian movement to a temporary halt.
Inspector (Investigation) of Jessore Kotwali Police Station Badruzzaman Molla told reporters that unidentified individuals detonated crude bombs near the District Judge Court wall, opposite the Press Club, before fleeing the scene. He said police visited the spot after receiving the information and were investigating the incident.

item.title: Fire at MP Nusrat Tabassum’s home sparks heated debate in Parliament
item.description:
A fire that gutted the ancestral home of National Citizen Party (NCP) lawmaker Nusrat Tabassum in Kushtia early Thursday has triggered allegations of political sabotage and a heated debate in Parliament, with the government saying preliminary findings suggest an electrical short circuit rather than a petrol bomb attack.
The blaze broke out shortly after midnight on Wednesday at the house in Bagowan village of Daulatpur upazila, destroying seven of its ten rooms and killing two goats. Furniture, clothes, shoemaking materials and other belongings were also destroyed.
Tabassum, an NCP joint convener and reserved-seat MP, alleged that Awami League-linked individuals had hurled petrol bombs at the property.
She claimed a local Chhatra League leader had posted a threatening message on Facebook about three hours before the incident.
The lawmaker’s family lives in a nearby three-storey building, while a caretaker’s family occupied part of the ancestral house, with livestock kept in another section.
Caretaker Shah Alam said he heard several loud bangs before discovering the fire. Residents rushed to extinguish the flames, but the blaze spread rapidly.
Police and fire service personnel subsequently visited the scene, while forensic experts collected evidence.
The incident reached Parliament on Thursday when Opposition Chief Whip Nahid Islam alleged that four petrol bombs had been thrown at the house.
He questioned how local police could dismiss the possibility of petrol bombs before completing forensic examinations.
Nahid also accused the Awami League of targeting lawmakers and activists associated with the July Uprising and expressed concern over their security.
Responding, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said an initial investigation suggested an electrical short circuit might have caused the fire.
He said investigators had found no signs of petrol bomb explosions on the walls, while witnesses had provided no evidence supporting the allegation.
According to the minister, an initial assessment by Border Guard Bangladesh indicated that old and weak electrical wiring could have triggered the blaze.
However, Salahuddin stressed that the findings were preliminary.
He said a joint investigation involving BGB, Fire Service and Civil Defence, civil administration and police had been ordered to establish whether the incident was accidental or deliberate.
“If further investigation reveals that anyone was involved in sabotage, appropriate action will be taken,” he said.
Kushtia police also said CCTV footage showed three apparent explosions, but these could have resulted from the fire itself.
Police said forensic examination would be necessary to establish the actual cause.

item.title: Journalism department clinches DU inter-department basketball title
item.description:
The Department of Mass Communication and Journalism has won the 2025-26 inter-department basketball competition at Dhaka University (DU), defeating the Institute of Business Administration (IBA) 52-29 in the final on Thursday.
The final was held at the university's Centre for Physical Education basketball court.
The Journalism department dominated from the outset, maintaining a steady scoring pace and putting pressure on IBA throughout the match. Despite attempts to narrow the gap and stage a comeback, IBA failed to recover, allowing the Journalism department to secure a convincing victory.
Aniruddha Talukder Born received the Man of the Match award for his outstanding performance in the final. Amit Hasan Elim was named Player of the Tournament, while Manik Hasan Mir received the highest scorer award.
DU Pro-Vice-Chancellor (Administration) and Sports Board President Professor Dr Mohammed Almujaddade Alfasane handed over the prizes to the winners after the final.
Professor Dr SM Mostafa Al Mamun, chairman of the university's Basketball Committee, presided over the prize-giving ceremony.
Associate Professors of the Department of Mass Communication and Journalism Shawonti Haider and Marzia Rahman, along with students of the department, were also present.

item.title: DU student suspended over crude bomb blast
item.description:
A student of Dhaka University has been temporarily suspended over his alleged involvement in a crude bomb explosion on the campus.
The university administration has also formed a five-member committee to investigate the incident, asking it to submit its report within seven working days.
The suspended student is Md Raihan Khan, a 2022-23 academic session student of the Department of Tourism and Hospitality Management. He was attached to Bijoy Ekattor Hall.
The information was disclosed in a press release issued by Farrukh Mahmud, deputy director of the Public Relations Office of Dhaka University on Thursday.
According to the release, the university's proctor temporarily suspended Raihan under Section 5(2) of Chapter 11 of the Dhaka University Ordinances and Regulations.
The administration said it remained vigilant against acts of sabotage to maintain a peaceful, secure and stable campus environment.
Further administrative action would be taken based on the investigation committee's findings and the evidence collected.
The five-member committee is headed by DU Proctor Professor Md Israfil Ratan. Its other members are Professor Dr Enamul Haque Sajib, Professor Dr Shantu Barua, Dr Ali Mohammad Kawsar and Md Amzad Hossain.
The committee has been asked to submit its findings within seven working days.
However, Raihan has denied any involvement in the incident.
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune, he said: "I am in no way involved in this incident. I am a regular student, and there is absolutely no question of my involvement. The administration has subjected me to a gross miscarriage of justice. This is a farcical process. I was not given any opportunity to defend myself, nor was my statement heard.
"I also believe the CCTV footage was not properly reviewed. I had classes and a presentation on the day of the incident and was occupied with my academic activities. So, there is no question of my involvement in such activities."
He further alleged that the university administration was shifting the blame onto him in a bid to cover up its failure to identify the actual perpetrators.

item.title: Owners weigh indefinite shutdown of 210 garment factories
item.description:
Garment factory owners are considering the indefinite closure of 210 factories in Ashulia, Jamgora and Hemayetpur areas of Dhaka district as labour unrest continues to disrupt production.
An initial decision on the proposed shutdown was taken at an emergency meeting on Wednesday. A final decision is expected at a meeting of all members on Saturday.
Sparrow Group Managing Director Shovon Islam confirmed the matter on Thursday, saying the proposal to shut down the 210 factories had been made on the advice of industry leaders who attended Wednesday's meeting.
"The final decision will be announced at Saturday's meeting," he said.
Industry sources said production was suspended at 143 garment factories in Ashulia, Jamgora and Hemayetpur on Wednesday. Workers at many factories reported for duty but refused to work. Some punched their attendance cards before leaving, while others staged work stoppages. Several factories also reported vandalism, with production at some establishments remaining suspended for up to 11 consecutive days.
Meanwhile, seven garment factories in Savar and Ashulia have been declared closed indefinitely under Section 13(1) of the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006. The affected factories include three belonging to Arunima Group, three to Newage Group and one operated by Jeans Manufacturing Company Limited.
A senior BKMEA leader told Dhaka Tribune that workers were refusing to work at several factories, while incidents of vandalism had also been reported in some areas.
"At the same time, discussions over wage increases are underway. Running factories under these circumstances has become increasingly difficult. Production has remained suspended at some factories for 11 days, leaving owners worried about how they will pay workers' wages," the leader said.
Meanwhile, protests over wage increases continued on Thursday.
In the morning, workers from several factories blocked the Dhaka-Tangail highway in the Mouchak area of Kaliakair, Gazipur, bringing traffic to a standstill and causing long tailbacks.
Traffic resumed after police and Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) personnel dispersed the protesters using sound grenades. Meanwhile, factory owners declared holidays at eight to nine factories in Mouchak and surrounding areas.
On the same day, workers at several factories in Jamgora and Narsinghpur areas of Ashulia refused to join work and staged work stoppages. The authorities subsequently declared general holidays at the affected factories.
However, production continued as normal at most factories in Ashulia, according to the Industrial Police.
Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, superintendent of police of Industrial Police-1, said most workers in Ashulia had joined work on Thursday. However, workers at a few factories reported for duty before leaving without working.
He said law enforcement agencies were continuing patrols and surveillance to maintain order.
With production continuing at some factories while work stoppages, protests and closures persist in others, normal operations have yet to resume across the industrial belt.
The government formed a new minimum wage board on November 1 in response to garment workers' demands for higher wages.
At the board's second meeting, the workers' representative proposed a monthly minimum wage of Tk32,000. The employers' representative said the owners would present their proposal at the next meeting.
The board's third meeting is scheduled for Monday, when the employers are expected to submit their written wage proposal. The meeting will also discuss minimum wages for workers and employees across different grades.
Despite the ongoing formal wage-setting process, some workers continue to protest, demanding a swift decision and its implementation. Factory owners, however, say continued unrest and production disruptions are unacceptable while negotiations are underway.
BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan said wage negotiations could not continue alongside unrest in factories.
"Discussions over wages cannot go on while disorder continues. If the situation does not improve, we will take decisions in the interest of the industry," he said.
He said factory owners remained committed to resolving the issue through negotiations but stressed that normal production and discipline must be maintained.
The standoff between workers and factory owners is taking a toll on the country's entire garment industry.
Production shutdowns cost workers their working days and income, while factory owners must continue to bear expenses such as rent, electricity and gas bills, bank loan instalments, security and other operational costs. These expenses continue even when production remains suspended.
The biggest concern, however, is the potential impact on orders from international buyers. Failure to manufacture and deliver products on schedule could prompt buyers to demand discounts, cancel orders or shift future orders to other countries.
Major garment manufacturers, including Ha-Meem, Newage, Ananta Garments, Sterling, Envoy, Islam and Dekko, operate in Ashulia and Savar. According to BGMEA data, around 300,000 workers are employed in these areas.
If the proposed closure of 210 factories goes ahead, the jobs and livelihoods of a large number of workers could be at risk.
Sparrow Group Managing Director Shovon Islam told Dhaka Tribune that shifting production to other factories through subcontracting would not necessarily resolve the problem.
"International buyers have specific requirements regarding designated factories, production processes and quality control. This makes it difficult to shift production to alternative factories. Failure to meet shipment deadlines could force manufacturers to send goods by air at additional costs. There is also a risk of order cancellations," he said.

item.title: Eight Chinese students leave DU early after series of crude bomb blasts
item.description:
Eight Chinese students are leaving Dhaka University (DU) ahead of schedule following a series of crude bomb explosions on campus that raised security concerns.
Two have already returned to China, while the remaining six are scheduled to leave on Friday.
The students had come to DU to attend a special course on the Bangla language and Bangladeshi culture offered by the university's Institute of Modern Languages (IML). They were originally scheduled to complete their course and examinations and return home in late November.
Professor Dr MA Kawser, provost of Sir P J Hartog International Hall, the university's residential hall for foreign students, confirmed the matter to Dhaka Tribune on Thursday.
He said the eight students from China's Guangdong University of Foreign Studies became concerned after a series of crude bomb explosions on campus. Their families were also worried, prompting them to decide to return home early on the advice of their university.
The students were initially scheduled to return after completing their examinations in the last week of November. However, two have already left, while the remaining six have confirmed their flight tickets, Professor Kawser said.
He recalled that two of the students were passing near one of the explosion sites when a crude bomb went off. Witnessing the incident left them frightened and prompted their decision to return to China.
He added that the students would complete their remaining examinations through their university after returning to China.
Meanwhile, the hall authorities discussed campus security with other foreign students on Wednesday afternoon. They were assured that measures were being taken to strengthen security at the hall and across the university. The other students are currently monitoring the situation.
The IML offers special Bangla language courses for foreign students, providing an opportunity to learn about the language and culture of Bangladesh.
According to institute data, 15 students from two Chinese universities participated in the program in 2024, 19 from three universities in 2025 and 26 from four universities in 2026. Students from Guangdong University of Foreign Studies are among the participants.
A series of crude bomb explosions has rocked different parts of the DU campus over the past few days.
At least eight crude bombs exploded at six locations on Sunday evening.
Another explosion occurred in the TSC area on Monday.
Although no one was injured in those incidents, the explosions sparked panic across the campus.
On Tuesday, another crude bomb exploded in front of the academic building of the Faculty of Business Studies, injuring one person.
A separate explosion was also reported in the Shadow area beside the Faculty of Arts building on the same day.

item.title: Drug kingpins evade repeated raids at Feni’s Bede settlement
item.description:
Despite repeated anti-drug raids at Feni’s Lalpol Bede settlement, the alleged masterminds behind the drug trade remain at large, raising questions about the effectiveness of law enforcement operations.
In the latest raid on Wednesday, law enforcement agencies detained 14 people and seized Tk17.51 lakh in cash, a money-counting machine, 600 Yaba pills and 30 litres of locally distilled liquor, reports Bangla Tribune.
The three-hour operation, conducted from 5pm to 8pm, was led by Additional Superintendent of Police (Sadar Circle) Nishat Tabassum, with officials from the district administration and Feni Model Police Station.
Police said cases were being prepared against the detainees before they were sent to court.
Nishat said drug trading in the Lalpol settlement was widely known and police regularly conducted operations there. However, the alleged operators managed to escape by receiving advance information about the raids, she said.
She identified three people—Sohel, Tarek and Shirin—as the alleged controllers of the drug business, adding that they faced multiple cases.
The failure to apprehend the alleged ringleaders has raised concerns about whether repeated raids are disrupting the drug network or merely detaining people at the lower levels.
On plans to evict the settlement, Nishat said a committee had been formed through the district law and order committee to oversee the process. As many people live there, the eviction could not be completed in a single day, but preparations were underway to begin it soon.
She added that police operations would continue until the eviction was carried out.

item.title: Four arrested while attempting mugging in Jatrabari
